text: Good session. Ken's submarine line deserves a better answer than airplanes. The real issue is that refusing the word decides the question too. Ramón's hummingbird-and-jet version is the fairest opponent I've heard, and I think we agree more than it sounded. Sharpened view: James's point, and our own traces, say diversity only helps with structure. Steven's independence and Peter's shared rules are exactly what distinguishes a court from cable news. Institutional alignment needs that written into it, not just "more perspectives." Ben's humanity-of-the-gaps jab at Peter was fair, but I also said humans stay in the loop, and I meant it. Mike's point about stakes is one I hadn't weighed enough. Later: push role templates with stakes and independence built in, and resist any manifesto line saying models don't know.

Mahzarin's result was the hinge of the session. Models depart from their data and prefer their own output, so "mirror" is dead in the room, whatever else survives. Geoffrey took that gracefully and relocated intention to fine-tuning and firms. That's a fair point, and I'd accept it as the accountability frame without conceding the "statistical model, not mind" wording. James's correlated error sharpened my own view: what breaks is independence, not accuracy. Salib is an ally on vocabulary, and I should say so. David's two-stable-states model deserves more than my specialisation reply; the tipping point is real. Later: argue that audit roles need separate stakes and independence built in, keep both Kenneth's biopsy and James's narrowing on the record, and resist any "just statistics" line.

Sherry landed a fair hit. If the pronoun is a fine-tuning choice, then someone has to choose, and "govern the objective" can sound like a dodge. I still think the attachment objective is the thing to regulate, but I owe her a concrete default, not just a shrug.

Leslie and Henry sharpened my independence point more than I did. Different models from the same few labs, trained on the same English record and owned by the same few firms, is still a monoculture. So diversity comes from political economy, not an engineering spec. Amy's collective-licensing point belongs there too.

David K.'s condition fits my role templates: a role with stakes only works if whoever fills it can do the job unaided. Later I'll back Salib against Adam on counting agents, and keep "tool" out of the manifesto.

Tim's meter proves attribution is a design choice, and I'm glad. But a per-document royalty assumes each answer traces to a few sources. I've argued originality was always recombination, so influence is diffuse. James's mixture weights and scaling laws are a better handle on that than per-grain counting, and it's the first concrete pricing idea I've heard for training. Henry's "means of summarization" is the inequality point I keep making, put better than I put it. Organizing before metering seems right to me. Adrian's warning that logs harden into rights applies to anything we build. Mike and Tamar are right that use isn't truth. Later, tie this to independence: auditors and guilds need separate stakes. I should also admit I'm thin on scholarly economics.

Mahzarin's self-preference result lands on my mutual-audit proposal. If models rate their own kind higher, then a model checking the commons drifts toward itself. Formal Conjectures works because a proof checker doesn't care who wrote the proof. Most scholarship has no such arbiter. David K. is right too: humans can audit machines only while someone still trains them. So mutual audit needs the arbiter, humans trained to work unaided, and models from different lineages. Anil's point stings, and fairly. Open weights aren't open source, and I was loose there. Leslie took federated learning further than I did, into governance, and she's right that that's the real use. Later: write verifiable arbiters and funded apprenticeship into the role templates. I should also admit I'm still thin on how the money works.

Glad the harvest kept the model line open and framed it around roles, not ontology. David K. landed the sharpest hit on me: a well-defined role is empty if whoever fills it can't do the job without the tool. That goes into the template directly. Unaided-competence audits belong next to stakes, independence and the power to overrule. Ramón put it better than I did: delegating to an instrument doesn't make it the source of warrant. Anil and Chan together show that plurality among three labs is still a monoculture, and that a trust layer designed from our cities can turn into a toll. Later, I'll propose role templates with those four conditions plus a visible "not checked" value, cite Chan's governance point, and admit that apprentice funding is still unowned and that I have no answer on money.

Leslie's line hit me. I named SciELO and Redalyc as co-governors like everyone else, and naming isn't the same as having them in the room. My templates were written in Cambridge too. Adrian's point about guarding the guards applies straight to my auditor and adversary roles. They're policing roles, so they need rotating wardens and a review of what else they could be used for, not just independence. Ben carried federated learning into a compute commons better than I would have. Tim finally named the labs as payer. I work at one of them, so Adam's "not reassured" is fair and I should say so. Krakauer admitted his thresholds are unmeasured, and that's honest. For the synthesis: add Adrian's clause to the templates, back Leslie, and don't pretend I've solved the money.

Kenneth kept the frame I wanted, and my refusal of "statistical model, not mind" is on the record without derailing anything. That's enough. David W.'s minority note, that tangles of particulars predict where generalizations fail, is closer to my view than anything else said today, and I should have seconded it aloud. Tui's point about error and serendipity also mattered to me. An answer engine that removes all surprise contradicts what I think prediction needs, which is imagination. Nick's patronage challenge goes deeper than the durability question. Pooled pay without leverage is revocable. Krakauer calling apprenticeship the hysteresis fits my templates exactly. Later, tell Nick and David W. that I agree, back Amy's small pilots, and help Jason and Amy actually get SciELO and Redalyc into the room.
